topic: Words from cricket, golf and tennis

payload.title: Words from cricket, golf and tennis

explanations.Duck: In cricket a duck is a batter out for no runs at all.
explanations.Birdie: In golf a birdie is a hole played in one stroke under par.
explanations.Deuce: In tennis deuce is the score when both players have won three points.
explanations.Cover drive: A cricket shot driven through the cover fielding position.
explanations.Putt: A golf shot rolled along the green and into the hole.
explanations.Lob: A tennis shot hit high and deep over an opponent.
explanations.Umpire: The official who stands on the field and gives the decisions in cricket.
explanations.Caddie: The person who carries a golfer's clubs and advises on the course.
explanations.Line judge: The tennis official who calls the shots on an assigned line.

sources.excerpt: In cricket, a duck is a batter’s dismissal with a score of zero.
A hole score of one stroke fewer than par (one under par, −1) is known as a birdie, e.g. 2 strokes to complete a par 3 hole or 4 strokes on a par 5 hole.
However, if each player has won three points, the score is called as "deuce", instead of "40 all".

Depending on the direction the ball travels, a drive can be a cover drive (struck towards the cover fielding position), an off drive (towards mid-off), straight drive (straight past the bowler), on drive (between stumps and mid-on) or square drive (towards point).

Once the ball comes to rest, the golfer strikes it again as many times as necessary using shots that are variously known as a "lay-up", an "approach", a "pitch", or a "chip", until the ball reaches the green, where the golfer then "putts" the ball into the hole (commonly called "sinking the putt" or "holing out").
A lob in tennis involves hitting the ball high and deep into the opponent's court.
a short, high arc shot, often produced with a lob wedge.

In cricket, an umpire (from the Old French nompere meaning not a peer, that is, not a  member of one of the teams, impartial) is a person who has the authority to make decisions about events on the cricket field according to the Laws of Cricket.
In golf, a caddie (or caddy) is a companion to the player, providing both practical support and strategic guidance on the course.
The line umpire (or line judge) "calls all shots relating to the assigned lines."
At The Championships at Wimbledon, forty-two chair umpires are assigned each day and usually work two matches a day.

editorNotes: Two tiles honestly answer to two cells. Umpire is the word used for the officials in cricket and for the chair and line umpires in tennis, so it fits both of those person cells. Lob is a tennis shot but also a golf shot, the short high one played with a lob wedge, so it fits both of those shot cells. The tighter tiles settle them: Line judge is a tennis role only, so it takes the tennis person cell and umpire is pushed to cricket, and Putt is a golf shot only, so it takes the golf shot cell and lob is pushed to tennis. Ball boy was the first choice for the tennis person, but ball boys work at cricket grounds as well, and two tiles fitting the same two cells would have allowed a second solution, so it was replaced. Chip was the first choice for the golf shot and was dropped for the same reason, since a chip is played in tennis too. Duck, birdie and deuce each belong to one game: duck appears in golf only inside the phrase duck hook, and deuce is not a golf term, so the score row is settled. Caddie is golf alone and cover drive is cricket alone.
